In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Integrative and distinctive coding of perceptual and conceptual object features in the ventral visual stream" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Timothy Behrens as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Anna C Schapiro (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

This paper aims to uncover where in the brain perceptual and conceptual information is integrated. The authors compare behavioral and neural similarity amongst objects processed in visual and conceptual task contexts. They find that visual structure is represented in LOC, conceptual structure is represented in the temporal pole and parahippocampal cortex, and that perirhinal cortex is uniquely sensitive to both perceptual and conceptual information, across task contexts, suggesting that this is where conceptual and perceptual information is integrated.

The reviewers commented on the elegant nature of the study design, the stringent analysis, and how clean results were in the context of brain areas that are often difficult to get signals from (with fMRI). The paper was judged to be of broad interest and impactful.

Essential revisions:

The following issues were highlighted as items that must be addressed before publication.

1) It looks like the statistics were computed using objects – not participants – as the random effects factor, which makes it unclear if we can generalize the findings to the population. The correlation between behavioral and neural RDMs could be calculated for each individual, and then statistical testing could be done across these 16 (fisher-transformed) values. Or it may make sense to run the permutation test within each individual and then compute group statistics across the 16 zscores of the individuals relative to their own null distributions. The object-based statistics are useful, but additionally reporting these participant-based statistics will allow the reader to understand whether these findings are likely to generalize to new participants.

2) These analyses tell us about how relationships between objects are represented similarly or differently in different task contexts, but it seems like it would be useful to also report how similarly the objects themselves are represented in different task contexts. In other words, in an RDM with visual brain response as rows and conceptual as columns, does perirhinal (and perhaps temporal pole) have the strongest diagonal in that matrix?

3) There looks to be a strong interaction effect in perirhinal cortex, with its patterns of activity showing more similarity to the behavior-based visual RDM vs. the behavior-based conceptual RDM when the task is visual, and vice versa when the task is conceptual. Could the authors assess this interaction? If the authors are concerned about the assumptions of an ANOVA being violated, then perhaps a non-parametric test of an interaction can be used. The presence of an interaction does not in any way contradict what the authors are stating, but would instead add to it by suggesting that, on top of PRC representing both conceptual and perceptual information regardless of task, there is a small modulation by the task state or attentional state.

4) There is something a little odd about the depiction of the visual and conceptual RDMs in Figure 1. Why are there vertical "streaks" though the columns? Shouldn't these RDMs be completely symmetrical? Perhaps this is an artifact of the normalization procedure, which is mentioned in the methods but not described in detail. As a general point, although it is fine to scale the RDMs to use the full light/dark range, I think that it would give a better idea of the similarity space if the actual values of the similarity measures were used rather than percentile scores. Also, in the uploaded RDMs, it is puzzling to me that the values for dissimilar pairs are all 1 for the visual RDM, as this was based on a 5-point Likert scale. Surely the same value wasn't obtained for every object pairing.

5) Although I think that the procedure used to obtain behavioral measures of conceptual and perceptual similarity is a strength of the paper, it would be useful to know how these measures compare to other measures of conceptual similarity, like WordNet distances, or text corpus co-occurrence, and whether similar results are obtained when these other measures are used.

6) Although the paper focuses primarily on the ROIs, the results of the searchlight analysis will be of considerable interest to many readers and deserve more emphasis. I suggest that the brains in Figure 7A and 7B be made larger (perhaps by removing the RDMs, which take up considerable space but aren't really essential). In addition, it would be useful to plot the borders of the ROIs as outlines on the brains so that the consistency between the ROI boundaries and the searchlight analyses could be visually assessed. (As an aside, the fact that PRC is the only area showing overlap between the visual and conceptual effects in the searchlight analysis is very impressive and really underscores the strength of the effect.)

7) The results in PHC are very interesting, but the use of the PHC ROI is not strongly justified in the paper, and the implications of this result are not discussed at all. Although the paper states that PHC has been implicated by previous work on conceptual knowledge, the papers that are referenced (by Bar and Aminoff, and Ranganath) discussed a very specific kind of conceptual knowledge: knowledge about co-occurrence of objects within the same context. In my opinion, an important aspect of the current results is that they offer an important new data point in support of this idea. One possible interpretation of the PHC results is that participants bring to mind a contextual setting for the object when they perform the conceptual tasks but not when they perform the perceptual tasks. For example, "comb" and "hairdryer" might bring to mind a bathroom or a barbershop, but only when thinking about the conceptual meaning of these objects, not when thinking about their shape or color.

8) It would be useful to have more precise information about the locus of the PHC effect relative to the "parahippocampal place area" (PPA), which tends to extend posterior of PHC proper. Several papers suggest an anterior/posterior division within the PPA whereby the more anterior portions represent more abstract/conceptual information and the more posterior portions represent more visual/spatial information (e.g. Baldassano et al., 2013; Marchette et al., 2015; Aminoff et al., 2006). The functional localizer includes both scenes and objects so it should be possible for the authors to identify the PPA, and thus report whether their effects are in PPA or not, and if so, if they are in the more anterior portion.

9) I wonder if the authors could comment on whether they think the results would change if pictures, rather than words, were used for the objects in the fMRI experiment. For example, might LOC represent visual similarity structure in a task-invariant way if pictures are presented, because their visual features would be processed more automatically than if words are presented, and visual features of the objects have to be brought to mind? I was also curious if the authors could explain their motivation for using words rather than images – was it to force participants to bring to mind both visual and conceptual information?

10) It is notable that conceptual effects were limited to PRC, PHC, and TP, and were not found in other regions of the brain. What implications does this have in light of previous work that has found a wider distribution of conceptual regions? For example, Fairhall and Caramazza (2013) identified "amodal" conceptual processing in inferior temporal gyrus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus, prefrontal regions? What about the ventral stream regions outside of LO, PRC, and PHC, like the fusiform gyrus? (I'm not actually suggesting that the authors use these regions as ROIs, but more focus on the whole-brain results and comparison to these earlier findings would be recommended.)

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Integrative and distinctive coding of visual and conceptual object features in the ventral visual stream" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Timothy Behrens (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

1) It was a great idea to put the ROI boundaries on the brains depicting the searchlight results. I'd recommend making the ROI borders a bit thicker, though, and perhaps changing their colors, to make them easier to see. The perirhinal and parahippocampal ROIs are fairly clear, but the LOC and temporal pole less so.

2) Now that the ROI outlines have been added to the searchlight results, it is apparent (Figure 10B) that the locus of conceptual decoding in parahippocampal cortex straddles the perirhinal/parahippocampal border. This fact is perhaps worth mentioning in the text. At present, the overlap with anterior PPA is emphasized, but one might equally emphasize that the overlap with PPA – and even PHC – is only partial.

3) Also, there seems to be an error in the caption for Figure 10B, which is described as depicting correlation between brain-based VISUAL and behavior-based conceptual RDMs – both should be conceptual. The label on the figure itself is different (and presumably correct).

results.result: Object concepts require integration of perceptual and conceptual features for full specification, as these features can vary independently across objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the theoretical foundation that object concepts are feature-based (C1), that visual and conceptual features can dissociate (C2), and that full specification requires integration (C3). These claims are supported by established theoretical frameworks and logical examples (e.g., hairdryer-gun vs. hairdryer-comb).

results.result: Competing theoretical frameworks propose that object features are coded in modality-specific regions, with debate over whether integration occurs through inter-regional interactions or trans-modal convergence zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 summarize established neurocognitive theories about feature representation, supported by multiple citations. These claims accurately characterize the theoretical landscape and competing views on how distributed features relate to object concepts.

results.result: Evidence from semantic dementia suggests the temporal pole supports multi-modal integration of conceptual but not perceptual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 synthesize neuropsychological evidence from semantic dementia showing that temporal pole damage leads to conceptual confusions (C10) but preserved visual discrimination, supporting the inference that this region integrates conceptual features (C11). Well-supported by citations to established research.

results.result: The representational-hierarchical model proposes perirhinal cortex integrates conceptual and perceptual features, but direct evidence remains elusive due to confounding of these features across stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 establish the theoretical motivation for the study. The representational-hierarchical model is well-cited (C12), parallel lines of evidence exist (C13-C14), but the critical limitation is identified: features typically covary (C15), making direct evidence of integration elusive (C16).

results.result: Behavior-based visual and conceptual similarity models were successfully constructed from independent participant samples, with visual and conceptual features orthogonal across object concepts.
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C84-C95 describe the construction and validation of behavior-based models. Large sample sizes (C84-C85), high data quality (C90), and systematic feature processing (C91-C94) support the models. Critically, C17 demonstrates orthogonality (tau=0.01, p=0.10), and C95 confirms robustness to feature inclusion decisions.

results.result: The word2vec corpus-based model captured both conceptual and visual similarity, suggesting it reflects broader semantic similarity than the behavior-based conceptual model.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 demonstrate that word2vec correlates with both behavior-based models (C18: tau=0.11, p<0.00001; C19: tau=0.04, p<0.001), supporting the inference (C20) that corpus-based models capture visual semantics in addition to conceptual features. Statistical evidence is clear.

results.result: Participants in the fMRI experiment (N=16) showed high consistency in property verification judgments across visual and conceptual task contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 demonstrate task validity: 88.4% agreement across all participants (C21), no difference between task contexts in agreement (C23, z=0.19, p=0.85) or response latencies (C24, t=1.00, p=0.33). Sample size (C86) is consistent with prior RSA studies but relatively small.

results.result: Lateral occipital cortex represents object concepts in a task-dependent visual similarity code, expressing visual similarity only when attention is directed to visual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26, C73 demonstrate task-dependent visual coding in LOC. In visual task context, brain RDMs correlated with visual model (C25: tau=0.045, p<0.002) but not conceptual model. In conceptual context, no significant correlations (C26). This pattern supports task-dependent visual representation.

results.result: Parahippocampal cortex represents object concepts in a task-dependent conceptual similarity code, expressing conceptual similarity only when attention is directed to conceptual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C74 demonstrate task-dependent conceptual coding in parahippocampal cortex. In conceptual task context, brain RDMs correlated with conceptual model (C29: tau=0.046, p<0.002) but not visual model. In visual context, no significant correlations (C28). Pattern supports task-dependent conceptual representation.

results.result: The temporal pole represents object concepts in a task-invariant conceptual similarity code, expressing conceptual structure regardless of task demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C43, C66-C67 demonstrate task-invariant conceptual coding in temporal pole. Brain RDMs correlated with conceptual model in both visual (C31: tau=0.035, p<0.001) and conceptual (C32: tau=0.05, p<0.0001) contexts. Within-object similarity was significant (C43: r=0.34, p<0.05), confirming task-invariance.

results.result: Perirhinal cortex uniquely represents object concepts in a task-invariant integrative similarity code that captures both visual and conceptual features in the same voxels.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C37, C44, C48-C56, C81-C82 provide converging evidence for integrative coding in PRC. ROI analysis shows correlations with both models in both contexts (C33). Searchlight analysis reveals PRC is the only region showing both visual and conceptual coding (C48, C55), with overlap in the same voxels (C49-C53). Within-object similarity significant (C44: r=0.41, p<0.01). This is the primary novel finding.

results.result: The word2vec model showed significant correlations with brain-based RDMs in multiple regions, including unexpected correlation with LOC visual task RDMs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 report word2vec correlations with brain data. Correlations with conceptual task RDMs in parahippocampal cortex, PRC, and temporal pole (C34) parallel behavior-based conceptual model results. Unexpected LOC correlation (C36) is consistent with word2vec capturing visual semantics (as shown in C19).

results.result: Brain-based RDMs from different ROIs were not significantly correlated with each other, suggesting distinct representational content across regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 demonstrate representational distinctiveness across ROIs. No significant correlations between visual task RDMs across ROIs (C39) or conceptual task RDMs across ROIs (C40). Visual and conceptual RDMs uncorrelated in LOC and parahippocampal cortex (C38). Statistical evidence is clear.

results.result: Within-object representations in LOC and parahippocampal cortex differed across task contexts, consistent with task-dependent coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 show within-object similarity did not differ from zero in LOC (r=0.007, p=0.20) and parahippocampal cortex (r=-0.008, p=0.87), indicating different representations across contexts. This is consistent with task-dependent coding observed in C25-C26 and C27-C29.

results.result: Whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed visual similarity coding in occipital and parietal regions, and conceptual similarity coding in temporal pole and parahippocampal/perirhinal border.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 report searchlight results that are largely consistent with ROI findings. Visual coding in LOC and other visual regions (C45), conceptual coding at parahippocampal/PRC border (C46), and bilateral temporal pole conceptual coding in both contexts (C47). Results supported by TFCE-corrected statistics.

results.result: Results demonstrate functional heterogeneity within the anterior temporal lobe, with temporal pole extracting conceptual features and perirhinal cortex integrating perceptual and conceptual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C69 synthesize findings to demonstrate ATL heterogeneity. The distinct patterns in temporal pole (conceptual only) versus PRC (integrative) support functional differentiation (C68). The inference that conceptual and perceptual information cannot be fully disentangled in PRC (C57) follows logically from the integrative coding pattern.

results.result: Prior research suggests fully specified object representations in PRC support discrimination among stimuli with high feature overlap and are important for memory judgments.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 review prior literature on PRC function. Multiple citations support the role of PRC in discriminating high-overlap stimuli (C58-C63) and memory for similar items (C64-C65). These claims provide context for interpreting the current integrative coding findings.

results.result: Perirhinal cortex has extensive connectivity with sensory regions, making it well-suited to serve as a trans-modal convergence zone for integrating visual and conceptual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 link anatomical connectivity to functional role. Extensive citations support PRC connectivity to temporal pole, parahippocampal cortex, LOC, and other sensory regions (C70). The inference that this connectivity supports trans-modal integration (C71) is reasonable given the observed integrative coding.

results.result: Attention may modulate multi-voxel activity patterns within and between regions, as evidenced by task-dependent effects in LOC and parahippocampal cortex and a trend toward interaction in PRC.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 propose attentional modulation. While task-dependent effects in LOC (C73) and parahippocampal cortex (C74) are well-supported, the claim is explicitly speculative (C72). The PRC interaction was only a trend (C75: p=0.082). The inference about multi-voxel modulation (C76) is reasonable but not definitively demonstrated.

results.result: Parahippocampal cortex may express conceptual similarity structure because conceptually similar objects co-occur in contexts, though this mechanism requires further investigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C80 propose a mechanism for parahippocampal cortex conceptual coding. While C77 is supported by data, the mechanistic explanation (C78-C80) is speculative. The study was not designed to test co-occurrence relationships (acknowledged in text), making this interpretation uncertain.

results.result: The overall pattern of results implicates perirhinal cortex in representing fully-specified object concepts through integration of visual and conceptual features.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 is the main conclusion, synthesizing results from multiple analyses. The convergent evidence from ROI-based RSA (C33), searchlight analysis (C48-C53), within-object similarity (C44), and cross-context correlations (C37) strongly supports this conclusion. This represents the primary contribution of the study.

results.result: Word stimuli were used to ensure both visual and conceptual features were extracted from pre-existing representations rather than bottom-up perceptual processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 justify the methodological choice to use words rather than pictures. The logic is sound: with words, both feature types are arbitrarily related to input (C88), whereas with pictures, visual features are directly accessible (C89). This design choice is appropriate for studying stored representations.
